changes.after: A normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped model. A cumulative probability is the share at or below a chosen value.

before: R commonly uses d for density or mass, p for cumulative probability, q for quantiles and r for random generation. pnorm(q, mean, sd) gives the probability at or below q under a specified normal model; a continuous density value is not the probability of one exact point.

A nondegenerate normal model is symmetric around its mean and has positive standard deviation; R also supports the special sd = 0 point-mass boundary, which is not used here. A calculation under that model does not establish that a real dataset is normal. Here the threshold equals the model mean, so half the probability lies below it.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
probability <- pnorm(10, mean = 10, sd = 2)
cat(sprintf("%.3f", probability), "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: 0.500. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Contrast pnorm with dnorm at the same threshold. You may trace it without a R interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped model. A cumulative probability is the share at or below a chosen value.
The chosen value equals the center, so half the model is on each side.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.

```r
probability <- pnorm(10, mean = 10, sd = 2)
cat(sprintf("%.3f", probability), "\n", sep = "")
```
The output is `0.500`. The probability is one half, shown to three decimal places.
Move both the center and the chosen value to twenty.
